science.title: Spatiotemporal evolution of urban livability amid China’s urban renewal: genetic algorithm projection pursuit and geographically weighted regression
science.description: Against the backdrop of the concurrent advancement of rapid urbanization and large-scale urban renewal, enhancing urban livability has become an important issue in China’s urban development. This study employs a Genetic Algorithm-optimized Projection Pursuit (GAPP) model to assess livability in 125 Chinese cities (2010–2022). Integrating spatial analysis and Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR), we investigate livability’s spatiotemporal evolution and the spatially heterogeneous impacts of urban renewal. Empirical findings reveal three major characteristics. First, urban livability exhibits robust spatial “disequilibrium and lock-in,” with coastal regions forming high-value clusters, while the Northwest and Northeast remain entrenched in cold spots. Second, regional divergence continues to widen, accompanied by a profound structural mismatch characterized by “macro-level convergence versus micro-level polarization.” Third, while urban renewal catalyzes livability improvement, its efficacy follows the law of diminishing marginal returns. Marginal improvements are pronounced in the baseline-depressed Northeast but severely diminish along the infrastructure-saturated southeastern seaboard. These findings validate the spatial non-stationarity of human habitat evolution. We argue that policymakers should abandon “spatially blind” physical expansion paradigms and instead promote context-specific organic renewal and asymmetric resource allocation to bridge regional livability divides.

science.title: Effects of genotype and exercise on hepatic gene expression in phenotype-selected marathon mice
science.description: Experimental evolution through selection experiments is a vital tool for exploring the special features of polygenic traits. Here, we provide liver transcriptome data from a paternally selected marathon mouse model (DUhTP), characterized by exceptional running performance, and unselected controls (DUC), both descended from the same polygenic background. To study training responses, both lines were either challenged by three weeks of high-speed treadmill training or remained sedentary. For each condition, eight animals were used for liver tissue isolation and next-generation sequencing. Raw sequencing files were submitted to the ArrayExpress collection under accession number E-MTAB-12071. High data quality was confirmed by appropriate mean read lengths, high mean quality scores, and low duplication rates after adapter trimming. With an average of 16.9 million reads per sample mapping to 19,930 genes, the dataset enables comprehensive gene expression analyses. A multiQC report for the dataset, together with a sample-by-gene count matrix, is available on Figshare. The provided data offer a valuable resource for research in polygenic traits associated with physical activity.

science.title: A transdiagnostic comparison of paranoia and cognitive-affective risk factors in Williams syndrome and schizophrenia spectrum disorders
science.description: Williams Syndrome (WS) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder marked by elevated social motivation and approach. Individuals with WS exhibit a distinctive cognitive-affective profile, including heightened anxiety, rigid thinking, and susceptibility to cognitive biases – all risk factors for disturbances of thought content such as paranoia. However, despite these risk factors, psychotic disorders are relatively uncommon in WS, raising the possibility that its social phenotype may mitigate clinically significant paranoia. We compared self-reported paranoia and associated cognitive-affective risk factors across individuals with WS (n = 19), schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD; n = 66), and healthy controls (HC, n = 70). Although both clinical groups exhibited elevated cognitive-affective risk factors relative to HC, individuals with WS reported less persecutory paranoia, more robust social networks, and less social avoidance than those with SSD, despite comparable social anxiety. In SSD, less robust social networks were associated with a stronger relationship between social-cognitive difficulties and persecutory paranoia than in WS. The Bias Against Disconfirmatory Evidence task revealed impaired belief updating in SSD, but relatively preserved belief updating in WS. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that social factors and belief updating may attenuate paranoia despite elevated risk factors, providing transdiagnostic insight into the social and cognitive processes shaping vulnerability to paranoia.
